message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 on consumer devices). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, and sophisticated control logic. | Simpler, more uniform cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work individually but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich instruction set (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for complex operations, branching, and varied data types. | Often a reduced instruction set tailored to SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations; many GPUs use a variant of the x86 or proprietary ISA. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers, low latency access. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory pools. |
| **Parallelism** | Mostly serial or limited parallelism (multithreading, hyper‑threading). | Massive data‑parallelism; thousands of threads can execute concurrently. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS services, general application code. | Tasks that can be expressed as many independent operations on large data sets: image/video processing, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power & heat** | Designed for lower power consumption per core; efficient at handling diverse workloads. | Higher power density; designed to deliver maximum throughput even if it consumes more power. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with single‑threaded or multithreaded code. | Requires parallel programming models (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan, Metal, etc.) or higher‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |

### Why the difference matters

- **Speed vs. flexibility**: CPUs are flexible and can handle almost any task quickly, but they’re not as fast as GPUs when you need to perform the same operation millions of times. GPUs excel at those repetitive, data‑parallel tasks because they can run many lightweight cores in lockstep.

- **Use cases**: If you’re building a web server, running a database, or developing a desktop application, a CPU is your main engine. If you’re rendering a 3D scene, training a neural network, or doing real‑time physics simulation, a GPU will dramatically accelerate the workload.

- **Cost & energy**: For most everyday computing, a CPU is cheaper and uses less power. For specialized compute‑heavy tasks, a GPU can reduce runtime by orders of magnitude, often justifying its higher cost and power draw.

In short, CPUs are generalists—good at a wide variety of tasks—but GPUs are specialists—super fast at highly parallel, repetitive tasks. That’s why modern systems combine both: the CPU handles the “control” flow, while the GPU takes over the heavy lifting for graphics or compute‑intensive workloads.
